plan: Two passages, weighted toward Key Ideas and Details (16 of 20) to address the section's KID shortfall. CLD-P-ACT-R-000072: original literary narrative (a sixty-eight-year-old grandmother learns to swim with her granddaughter's help; third-person narration). CLD-P-ACT-R-000073: natural science on unihemispheric sleep (dolphins; Rattenborg's 1999 mallard study; northern fur seals; the 2016 frigatebird flight study). Topics checked against both workstreams (no matches). Difficulty provisional.

passages.title: The Far Wall
passages.text:
Marisol Reyes had driven a city bus for thirty-one years, and in all that time she had never once been late. She was proud of that record, and of most things about her life, but there was one fact she kept to herself: at sixty-eight, she could not swim. She had grown up in a dry inland town where the only standing water was a cattle tank, and by the time she moved to the coast, the moment for learning seemed to have passed.

It was her granddaughter, Tess, who found out. They were at the community pool on a July afternoon, Tess swimming laps and Marisol sitting on a bench with a newspaper, when Tess called for her to come in. Marisol said the water looked cold. Tess said it was eighty-two degrees. Marisol said she had forgotten her swimsuit. Tess pointed out that she was wearing it under her dress. There was a pause long enough that Tess climbed out of the pool, sat down beside her, and asked, very quietly, "Abuela, can you swim?"

Marisol had expected to feel embarrassed. Instead she felt something closer to relief, as if she had been carrying a heavy bag for years and someone had finally offered to take one handle. "No," she said. "Never learned." Tess, who was fifteen and taught swimming to small children at the same pool every Saturday, considered this. "I could teach you," she said. "I teach five-year-olds. You can't be worse than five-year-olds." "You'd be surprised," Marisol said.

The first lessons did not go well. Marisol could not make herself put her face in the water; every time she tried, her body seemed to decide for her, jerking her head back up before her nose was wet. Tess did not push. She had Marisol stand in the shallow end and blow bubbles, then hold the wall and kick, then float on her back while Tess kept one hand flat beneath her shoulders. "The water wants to hold you up," Tess said. "You just have to let it." Marisol thought this was the kind of thing people said to five-year-olds, but she noticed that it worked anyway.

By the end of August, Marisol could swim the width of the pool, slowly, with her chin held high like a woman crossing a busy street. She was not graceful, and she knew it. But on the last Saturday of the summer, she arrived early, before Tess's class of five-year-olds, and swam the whole length of the pool alone. When she reached the far wall and turned around, she saw that the children had gathered at the edge to watch, and that Tess was standing behind them with her arms folded, trying not to smile.

"Show-off," Tess said. "Thirty-one years," Marisol said, catching her breath, "and I was never late. I'm not about to start now."

passages.title: Half Asleep
passages.text:
For most animals, including people, sleep is an all-or-nothing affair: when we fall asleep, both halves of the brain slow down together. But some animals have found a way around this. Dolphins, for example, can rest one half of the brain at a time while the other half stays alert. During this "unihemispheric" sleep, the eye connected to the waking half of the brain typically stays open, and the dolphin keeps swimming and surfacing to breathe.

Birds do something similar. In a 1999 study, the neuroscientist Niels Rattenborg and his colleagues placed mallard ducks in a row and recorded their brain activity as they slept. Ducks in the middle of the row tended to sleep with both halves of the brain at once. Ducks at the ends of the row, however, more often slept with one half of the brain awake, and they tended to keep open the eye facing away from the other ducks, toward the direction from which a predator would most likely approach. The finding suggested that the birds could control which half of the brain stayed alert, depending on where danger was likely to come from.

Some animals change the way they sleep depending on their surroundings. Northern fur seals sleep with both halves of the brain when they rest on land. At sea, however, they mostly use unihemispheric sleep, often floating on one side while paddling with one flipper to keep their nostrils above the water.

The most dramatic example may be the great frigatebird, a seabird that can stay aloft over the ocean for weeks at a time. For years, scientists wondered whether frigatebirds slept in flight at all. In 2016, Rattenborg's team attached small devices that recorded brain activity to frigatebirds in the Galápagos Islands. The birds did sleep while flying, sometimes with one half of the brain and sometimes with both, but only in brief bursts that added up to about forty minutes a day. On land, the same birds slept more than twelve hours a day.

These findings raise as many questions as they answer. If half a brain's worth of sleep is enough for a dolphin, researchers wonder, why do other animals, including humans, sleep with the whole brain at once? One possibility is that sleeping with both halves allows the brain to recover more efficiently, so that animals sleep this way whenever it is safe to do so. For now, though, the frigatebird's forty minutes remain a puzzle: no one knows how the birds manage on so little sleep, or what, if anything, it costs them.

candidates.stem: The passage mainly focuses on:

choices.A: a teenager's efforts to train young children to swim in competitions.
choices.B: a grandmother's experience of learning to swim with her granddaughter's help.
choices.C: a family's disagreement about whether a grandmother should retire from work.
choices.D: a woman's memories of growing up in a dry town far from the coast.

candidates.evidence: It was her granddaughter, Tess, who found out
candidates.explanation: The passage follows Marisol from hiding that she cannot swim, through Tess's lessons, to swimming the length of the pool.

A.rationale: Tess teaches young children, but the passage focuses on Marisol.

D.rationale: Her childhood is mentioned only briefly to explain why she never learned.

hints: Who changes most over the course of the passage?

strategy.explanation: Summarize the beginning, middle, and end.

candidates.remember: A main-idea answer covers the whole passage.

candidates.stem: According to the passage, Marisol had never learned to swim mainly because she:

choices.A: grew up where there was little water and later felt it was too late to learn.
choices.B: was afraid of the cattle tank that was the only standing water in her hometown.
choices.C: was too busy driving a city bus for thirty-one years to take swimming lessons.
choices.D: had never been invited to the community pool by her family.

candidates.evidence: by the time she moved to the coast, the moment for learning seemed to have passed
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 1 says she grew up in a dry inland town and that by the time she moved to the coast, the moment for learning seemed to have passed.

B.rationale: The cattle tank is mentioned only as the town's one source of standing water.

C.rationale: Her bus-driving career is not given as the reason.

D.rationale: Nothing suggests this; the passage gives a different reason.

hints: What two facts does paragraph 1 give about her past?
candidates.remember: Answer detail questions from the text itself.

candidates.stem: Marisol's remarks about the cold water and her forgotten swimsuit (paragraph 2) most strongly suggest that she:

choices.A: genuinely disliked the community pool and its crowds.
choices.B: had truly forgotten that she was wearing her swimsuit.
choices.C: wanted Tess to stop swimming laps and go home.
choices.D: was trying to avoid revealing that she could not swim.

candidates.evidence: There was a pause long enough that Tess climbed out of the pool
candidates.explanation: Each excuse is answered, and the long pause leads Tess to guess the real reason: Marisol cannot swim and has been hiding it.

A.rationale: She came to the pool with Tess; the remarks are excuses, not complaints about the pool.

B.rationale: Tess points out the suit, and the long pause that follows suggests the excuses were cover.

C.rationale: Nothing suggests she wanted to leave.

hints: Why might someone give several excuses in a row?

strategy.explanation: Look at what follows the excuses.

candidates.remember: A character's excuses often hide a reason the character will not state.

author_checklist.hardness: must infer motive from a sequence of excuses

candidates.stem: The comparison of Marisol's secret to "a heavy bag" (paragraph 3) mainly suggests that:

choices.A: Marisol had been carrying too many things to the pool that day.
choices.B: Tess was now responsible for keeping the secret from the family.
choices.C: keeping the secret had been a burden that sharing it began to ease.
choices.D: Marisol regretted telling Tess and wanted to take the words back.

candidates.evidence: she felt something closer to relief
candidates.explanation: Having someone "take one handle" of a heavy bag suggests relief at sharing a burden she had carried alone.

A.rationale: The bag is figurative, not a real bag.

B.rationale: Nothing suggests Tess must keep it secret.

hints: What feeling does Marisol have in place of embarrassment?

strategy.explanation: Connect the image to the feeling named just before it.

candidates.remember: Interpret an image through the feeling it describes.

candidates.stem: Tess's remark "You can't be worse than five-year-olds" (paragraph 3) is best described as:

choices.A: a serious criticism of Marisol's ability to learn new physical skills at her age.
choices.B: a teasing comment meant to make the idea of lessons feel less intimidating.
choices.C: a complaint about how difficult her Saturday students are to teach.
choices.D: a polite way of refusing to give Marisol swimming lessons.

candidates.evidence: "I could teach you," she said
candidates.explanation: Tess offers lessons and then jokes that Marisol cannot do worse than small children, lightening an awkward moment.

A.rationale: The remark is playful; Tess has just offered to teach her.

C.rationale: Tess is not complaining about her students.

D.rationale: Tess has just offered to teach her.

hints: What has Tess just offered to do?

strategy.explanation: Read the remark with the offer before it.

candidates.remember: Tone depends on what a speaker is trying to accomplish.

candidates.stem: According to paragraph 4, which of the following did Tess do during the first lessons?

choices.A: She kept a hand beneath Marisol's shoulders while Marisol floated on her back.
choices.B: She insisted that Marisol put her face in the water from the very first lesson.
choices.C: She had Marisol practice kicking in the deep end of the pool.
choices.D: She asked her Saturday students to show Marisol how to float.

candidates.evidence: Tess kept one hand flat beneath her shoulders
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 4 lists the steps of the early lessons, including floating on her back with Tess's hand beneath her shoulders.

B.rationale: Tess "did not push" when Marisol could not put her face in the water.

C.rationale: Marisol practiced in the shallow end and at the wall.

D.rationale: The students are not part of the early lessons.

hints: What steps does paragraph 4 list?
candidates.remember: Check each choice against the specific paragraph named.

candidates.stem: Marisol's reaction to Tess's statement that "the water wants to hold you up" (paragraph 4) suggests that Marisol:

choices.A: rejected the advice and stopped taking lessons for a time.
choices.B: considered the advice childish but found that it helped her anyway.
choices.C: believed that the advice was the only thing she needed to learn.
choices.D: thought Tess was repeating something Marisol had told her years before.

candidates.evidence: but she noticed that it worked anyway
candidates.explanation: Marisol thinks the line is meant for five-year-olds, yet she notices that it works.

A.rationale: She continues the lessons and the advice works.

C.rationale: She thinks the advice sounds childish, not that it is complete.

hints: What two things does Marisol think about the advice?

strategy.explanation: Read the sentence after the advice.

candidates.remember: Watch for "but" signaling a change in a character's view.

candidates.stem: The description of Marisol swimming "with her chin held high like a woman crossing a busy street" (paragraph 5) mainly suggests that she swam:

choices.A: quickly, as if hurrying to catch a bus on time.
choices.B: proudly, in order to show off for the children watching.
choices.C: cautiously and with determination rather than with ease.
choices.D: carelessly, without paying attention to others in the pool.

candidates.evidence: She was not graceful, and she knew it
candidates.explanation: Someone crossing a busy street moves carefully and steadily; together with "slowly" and "not graceful," the image shows effortful determination.

A.rationale: She swims "slowly"; the image is about care, not speed.

B.rationale: The children have not yet appeared when she swims the width of the pool.

D.rationale: Crossing a busy street with chin held high suggests alertness, not carelessness.

hints: What words near the image describe how she swam?

strategy.explanation: Use the nearby words to interpret the image.

candidates.remember: Interpret a simile using the details around it.

author_checklist.hardness: simile with a tempting literal-association trap

candidates.stem: Which of the following events occurs first in the passage?

choices.A: Marisol swims the whole length of the pool alone.
choices.B: Marisol practices blowing bubbles in the shallow end.
choices.C: Tess's students gather at the edge of the pool to watch.
choices.D: Tess asks Marisol whether she can swim.

candidates.evidence: "Abuela, can you swim?"
candidates.explanation: Tess's question in paragraph 2 comes before the lessons and the final swim.

A.rationale: This happens at the end of the summer.

B.rationale: This happens during the first lessons, after Tess asks.

C.rationale: This happens on the last Saturday of the summer.

hints: Which paragraph contains each event?
candidates.remember: Track the order of events by paragraph.

candidates.stem: Marisol's final remark connects her swimming to her bus-driving career mainly by suggesting that she:

choices.A: takes the same pride in being on time that she took in her job.
choices.B: wishes she had learned to swim while she was still driving a bus.
choices.C: plans to return to work now that she has learned to swim.
choices.D: thinks Tess is wrong to call her a show-off for swimming alone.

candidates.evidence: and I was never late. I'm not about to start now
candidates.explanation: Arriving before the class, she jokes that she has never been late and will not start now, echoing the pride in her bus-driving record from paragraph 1.

C.rationale: Nothing suggests she plans to return to work.

D.rationale: She answers the teasing with a joke about punctuality rather than disputing it.

hints: What fact from paragraph 1 does the remark echo?

strategy.explanation: Connect the last line to the first paragraph.

candidates.remember: Endings often echo details from the opening.

author_checklist.hardness: must connect the closing line to the opening detail

candidates.stem: The passage is primarily concerned with:

choices.A: arguing that humans could learn to sleep with only one half of the brain at a time.
choices.B: explaining how scientists record the brain activity of wild animals as they sleep.
choices.C: describing animals that sleep with half the brain and what they suggest about sleep.
choices.D: comparing the hunting methods of dolphins, ducks, fur seals, and seabirds.

candidates.evidence: some animals have found a way around this
candidates.explanation: The passage presents dolphins, ducks, fur seals, and frigatebirds as animals that sleep with half the brain, then considers the questions they raise.

A.rationale: The passage never suggests humans could learn this.

B.rationale: The recording devices are mentioned only briefly.

D.rationale: The passage compares sleep, not hunting.

hints: What do all the animals in the passage have in common?
candidates.remember: A main-idea answer must cover every paragraph.

candidates.stem: According to the passage, during unihemispheric sleep a dolphin typically:

choices.A: closes both eyes but continues to swim slowly near the surface.
choices.B: keeps open the eye connected to the waking half of its brain.
choices.C: stops swimming and floats on its side with one flipper raised.
choices.D: sleeps with both halves of the brain for a few minutes at a time.

candidates.evidence: the eye connected to the waking half of the brain typically stays open
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 1 says the eye connected to the waking half stays open while the dolphin keeps swimming.

A.rationale: The passage says the eye connected to the waking half stays open.

C.rationale: This describes fur seals at sea, not dolphins.

D.rationale: Unihemispheric sleep rests one half at a time.

hints: What does paragraph 1 say about the dolphin's eyes?
candidates.remember: Do not confuse details about different animals.

candidates.stem: According to the passage, the ducks at the ends of the row differed from those in the middle in that the ducks at the ends:

choices.A: slept for longer periods than the ducks in the middle.
choices.B: kept open the eye that faced toward the other ducks.
choices.C: never slept with both halves of the brain at once.
choices.D: more often slept with one half of the brain awake.

candidates.evidence: Ducks at the ends of the row, however, more often slept with one half of the brain awake
candidates.explanation: The ducks at the ends more often used unihemispheric sleep than those in the middle.

A.rationale: The passage does not compare how long they slept.

B.rationale: They kept open the eye facing away from the other ducks.

C.rationale: They did so less often, not never.

hints: What does "however" contrast in paragraph 2?
candidates.remember: Watch for answers that reverse a detail or turn "more often" into "never."

candidates.stem: The passage suggests that the ducks at the ends of the row kept open the eye facing away from the group because:

choices.A: that was the direction from which danger was most likely to come.
choices.B: light from that direction was dimmer and easier for them to tolerate.
choices.C: the ducks in the middle of the row were blocking their view in the other direction.
choices.D: that eye was connected to the half of the brain that needed more sleep.

candidates.evidence: toward the direction from which a predator would most likely approach
candidates.explanation: Ducks at the ends of the row had no birds on their outer side, so a predator would most likely come from there, and they kept that eye open.

C.rationale: The passage gives danger, not a blocked view, as the reason.

D.rationale: The open eye is connected to the waking half, not the half needing sleep.

hints: What lay beyond the outer side of an end duck?

strategy.explanation: Connect the open eye to the predator detail.

candidates.remember: Inferences should rest on stated details.

author_checklist.hardness: must combine row position with the predator detail

candidates.stem: According to the passage, northern fur seals use unihemispheric sleep mainly when they are:

choices.A: on land.
choices.B: feeding.
choices.C: at sea.
choices.D: migrating.

candidates.evidence: At sea, however, they mostly use unihemispheric sleep
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 3 says fur seals sleep with both halves on land but mostly unihemispherically at sea.

A.rationale: On land they sleep with both halves of the brain.

hints: Where do fur seals sleep with both halves of the brain?
candidates.remember: Read the contrast word "however" carefully.

candidates.stem: The main function of paragraph 3 is to:

choices.A: explain why fur seals cannot sleep safely on land without keeping one eye open.
choices.B: show that some animals change the way they sleep depending on where they are.
choices.C: describe the method Rattenborg used to study sleeping ducks.
choices.D: argue that seals sleep less than any other animal in the passage.

candidates.evidence: Some animals change the way they sleep depending on their surroundings
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 3's first sentence states its point, and the fur seal is the example.

A.rationale: The paragraph says they sleep with both halves on land.

C.rationale: The duck study is in paragraph 2.

D.rationale: The paragraph does not compare amounts of sleep.

hints: What does the first sentence of paragraph 3 say?
candidates.remember: A paragraph's opening sentence often states its function.

candidates.stem: Based on the passage, how did the frigatebirds' sleep in flight compare with their sleep on land?

choices.A: They slept about the same amount in both settings.
choices.B: They slept more in flight because flying was restful.
choices.C: They slept only with one half of the brain on land.
choices.D: They slept far less in flight than they did on land.

candidates.evidence: On land, the same birds slept more than twelve hours a day
candidates.explanation: About forty minutes a day in flight compared with more than twelve hours on land shows they slept far less in flight.

A.rationale: About forty minutes a day in flight is far less than twelve hours on land.

C.rationale: The passage does not describe how their brains slept on land.

hints: What two amounts of sleep does paragraph 4 give?
candidates.remember: Compare quantities directly.

candidates.stem: According to paragraph 4, which of the following did the 2016 study find about frigatebirds sleeping in flight?

choices.A: They slept in brief bursts, sometimes with both halves of the brain.
choices.B: They never slept at all while flying for long periods over the ocean.
choices.C: They slept only with one half of the brain at a time, never with both.
choices.D: They slept in long periods, each lasting several hours, while gliding.

candidates.evidence: sometimes with one half of the brain and sometimes with both
candidates.explanation: Paragraph 4 says the birds slept in brief bursts, sometimes with one half of the brain and sometimes with both.

B.rationale: The study found that they did sleep in flight.

C.rationale: They sometimes slept with both halves.

D.rationale: They slept only in brief bursts.

hints: How long were the bursts, and which halves of the brain slept?
candidates.remember: Watch for choices that turn "sometimes" into "only" or "never."

candidates.stem: Which of the following questions does the passage indicate remains unanswered?

choices.A: Do dolphins rest one half of the brain at a time?
choices.B: Do frigatebirds sleep at all while they are flying over the ocean?
choices.C: How do frigatebirds manage to function on so little sleep?
choices.D: Where do northern fur seals use unihemispheric sleep?

candidates.evidence: no one knows how the birds manage on so little sleep
candidates.explanation: The last paragraph says no one knows how frigatebirds manage on so little sleep; the other questions are answered in the passage.

B.rationale: The 2016 study found that they do.

D.rationale: Paragraph 3 answers this: mostly at sea.

hints: Which question does the last paragraph say no one can answer?
candidates.remember: Distinguish questions a passage answers from those it leaves open.

author_checklist.hardness: requires checking each question against what the passage settles

candidates.stem: As it is used in paragraph 4, the word "dramatic" most nearly means:

choices.A: theatrical.
choices.B: striking.
choices.C: emotional.
choices.D: sudden.

candidates.evidence: The most dramatic example may be the great frigatebird
candidates.explanation: The frigatebird is the most remarkable, or striking, example of sleep with half the brain.

A.rationale: The frigatebird is not performing; this is the stage sense of the word.

C.rationale: Nothing about the example involves emotion.

D.rationale: The example is remarkable, not sudden.

hints: What makes the frigatebird stand out from the other examples?

strategy.explanation: Substitute each choice into the sentence.

candidates.remember: Choose the meaning that fits the context.
